visuals.heading: Not the Same As a Job Search

items.text: "How do I get hired" is a tactics problem: resumes, portals, referrals, interview prep.
A direction is not a map with every turn marked.
Skipping self-assessment and jumping straight to "which industry is booming" is the single most common reason a career plan collapses within a year.
Use three layers together - call it The Direction Compass - because any one of them alone gives a distorted read.
Not abstract ideals - the concrete things you will not sacrifice for a bigger title or a bigger number.

blocks.heading: Test a Direction Before You Commit

items.text: The most expensive mistake in this whole process is not picking the "wrong" direction.

Before committing serious time or money to a direction, run a small, low-risk test: a two-to-four-week freelance task, a short internship, a volunteer project, or even a few hours of real, unpaid work shadowing someone doing the job.
If a paid course or program is part of your test, judge the specific course, not the platform's name or star rating.

blocks.heading: Adjusting the Plan As You Learn

items.text: A career direction that is never rechecked is not a plan - it is a guess frozen in time.
Look at the evidence, not the emotion
Direction decisions made from a bad week are usually wrong; direction decisions made from a pattern across months are usually right.

blocks.heading: Mistakes That Derail Early Career Direction

items.text: Chasing a specific designation copied from a topper, a cousin, or a LinkedIn post skips the actual question: what problem do you want to get good at solving.
A first job that turns out to be a weak fit is expensive to sit inside out of guilt, but it is rarely permanent.
Clarity about your career direction after graduation usually arrives after you have done real, specific work, not before. Waiting for certainty first is one of the slower ways to build it.

blocks.heading: Setting a 3-5 Year Direction Without Over-Planning

items.text: Locks in one job title, five years out, before you have real market information.
Treats a change of mind at year two as failure instead of new data.
Ignores chance conversations, unexpected offers, and skills you did not know you had until you tried them.
Creates panic when the plan does not match reality on schedule.
Highest number on the offer letter wins, regardless of what the daily work actually involves.
No real check on who you would report to, what they measure, or whether they invest time in juniors.
Skill growth is assumed, not verified against the actual role scope.
A slightly better number today can lock you into a narrow, low-learning track for years.

blocks.heading: Degree or Certification Before Deciding Your Direction

items.text: Law, medicine, chartered accountancy, actuarial science, teaching, architecture, and similar fields entry requirement entry by a formal degree, licence, or supervised practice - there is no self-taught shortcut around this.
Plan your education budget around it directly.
Even here, a degree alone rarely builds the full picture - pair it with real practical exposure (clinics, internships, moot courts, articleship) wherever the course allows it.
